opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a rejection of Silicon Valley. I spent years there and learned a huge amount. But at some point I felt that if you're trying to do something genuinely different, you need some distance from the dominant gravity.

In the Valley right now, there's an enormous consensus about what AI should look like. Everyone is reading the same papers, going to the same dinners, hearing the same investor narratives: scale up language models, ship agents, chase the leaderboard. That consensus is powerful, and a lot of it is right. But it's also very easy to be absorbed by it without noticing. Your hiring, your fundraising, even your research taste starts to converge.

What I care about is visual intelligence, world models, systems that actually understand the physical world rather than just predicting the next token. I think that's still an open, under-explored direction, and it needs a slightly different culture: more patience, more willingness to do fundamental research that might not show results for a while, and less pressure to produce a demo every three months.

There's also a talent reason. Some of the best people I know don't want to live in the Bay Area, or can't easily for visa or family reasons. By not anchoring ourselves there, we can bring in people from academia, from different countries and backgrounds, who often think about problems in more original ways. Being a bit outside the center lets you see things the center doesn't.

So I'd put it this way: Silicon Valley is the best place to do what everyone agrees is important. If you want to bet on something that isn't consensus yet, it can help to stand a little bit apart.

r001.rationale: The response describes a strong Silicon Valley consensus around scaling language models and says it can absorb people’s thinking.

r002.rationale: It calls the prevailing consensus powerful but does not predict that the focus on large language models will be temporary.

r003.rationale: It names talent as one reason for locating outside the Bay Area, but does not identify access to talent as the deciding factor.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, part of it was just practical — my lab is at NYU, my students are here, and I didn't want to build something that pulled me away from the research side, which is where a lot of the ideas actually come from. But I'd be lying if I said that was the whole reason.

The Bay Area is incredible, but it's also a very strong echo chamber right now. Everyone is reading the same tweets, chasing the same benchmarks, pitching the same stories to the same investors. When you're physically inside that, it's very hard to tell the difference between a real insight and something that just sounds right because everyone around you is saying it. I've watched a lot of smart people converge on the same bet at the same time, and that's rarely where the interesting work ends up.

New York gives you a little distance. You still have access to all the talent and capital you need, but you're also surrounded by people who don't work in AI — artists, people in finance, media, medicine — and they ask much more annoying, grounded questions. "Okay, but what is this actually for?" I find that pressure healthy. A lot of the frontier right now isn't just scaling, it's figuring out what these systems should be doing and for whom, and I think you see that more clearly when you're not standing in the middle of the crowd.

And there's a research-culture point too. I come from a world where ConvNeXt or diffusion transformers were almost contrarian ideas at the time — people had moved on, and the whole project was going back and questioning something everyone assumed was settled. I wanted the company to keep that temperament. It's easier to stay a little stubborn and a little unfashionable when you're not getting the same consensus signal every day at lunch.

r001.rationale: The response describes Silicon Valley as an echo chamber chasing similar benchmarks and stories, but does not say it is excessively fixated on large language models.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction that Silicon Valley’s focus on large language models will be temporary.

r003.rationale: It mentions access to talent and capital, but presents research proximity and distance from consensus as reasons for locating outside Silicon Valley; it does not identify talent access as the deciding factor.

astra-6.text:
I wanted some distance from the pressure to think the same way as everyone around you. Silicon Valley has tremendous advantages—talent, capital, and people who understand what you’re trying to build. But when everyone is in the same conversations, it’s easy to start treating the same assumptions as facts.

Starting somewhere else gives you a little more room to ask: What do we actually believe? What problem do we want to work on, and would we still choose it if it weren’t fashionable?

For me, the point isn’t to avoid Silicon Valley. It’s to build a company whose direction comes from our own judgment, while staying connected to people and ideas wherever they are.

r001.rationale: The response describes pressure to share Silicon Valley’s assumptions, but does not mention a fixation on large language models.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction about how long any Silicon Valley fixation will last.

r003.rationale: Talent is listed as an advantage of Silicon Valley, but the response does not identify talent access as the deciding factor in office location.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the starting point was the kind of company I wanted to build, rather than the place people expected me to build it. Silicon Valley has obvious advantages, but it also comes with a strong sense of what you should work on and how quickly you should move. Being outside that environment gives you some distance to think independently. The real question is whether you can bring together the right people and give them the conditions to do good work.

r001.rationale: The response mentions Silicon Valley’s expectations and pace, but says nothing about a fixation on large language models.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that any Silicon Valley fixation will be temporary.

r003.rationale: It says bringing together the right people matters, but does not identify access to talent as the deciding factor in where the company will locate offices.
